newsitem.title: UK: IRA calls new truce to get Sinn Fein to talks.
newsitem.headline: IRA calls new truce to get Sinn Fein to talks.

text.p: The IRA on Saturday announced a new truce in its war against British rule of Northern Ireland in a move to get its political wing, Sinn Fein, to peace talks from which it has been barred by IRA violence for 13 months.

The ceasefire, which takes effect at noon on Sunday, was announced by the Irish Republican Army's ruling Army Council in a statement to the Irish media which said "all IRA units have been instructed accordingly."

"The IRA is committed to ending British rule in Ireland. It is the root cause of division and conflict in our country. We want a permanent peace and therefore we are prepared to enhance the search for a democratic peace settlement through real and inclusive political negotiations," the statement said.

Britain and Ireland, sponsors of the talks between Protestant Unionists, who want the province to stay British, and Catholic Irish nationalists, welcomed the move but said it was only a step on the road to an elusive political settlement.

Hardline Unionists, who fear that Britain has bent over backwards to ensure the inclusion of Sinn Fein, hinted they might walk out of the talks, which resume next week before substantive negotiations commence in September.

But the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), the most powerful voice of the pro-British Protestant majority, gave the move a guarded welcome and awaited talks between its leader, David Trimble, and British Prime Minister Tony Blair on Monday.
Martin McGuinness, de facto deputy to Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams, urged Unionists not to dwell on the past.
"What we need are real negotiations, not useless recriminations," he told a Belfast news conference. "We all need to declare ceasefires in our minds."

It was the second IRA ceasefire since the guerrillas called a "complete cessation" in August 1994 which they broke off in February 1996 with a new bombing campaign after failing to get invited to the Belfast peace talks.
In 1994 Catholics rallied in huge numbers across the province in "victory celebrations." But this time the response was muted and the turnout for similar demonstrations was lower on Saturday.

Adams said the key to the IRA's truce was British assurances that the Anglo-Irish guardians of the talks would not allow the issue of surrendering IRA arms to torpedo discussion of a political settlement.

Instead, "decommissioning" will be discussed in parallel with Anglo-Irish proposals to devolve some power to Northern Ireland and establish cross-border bodies to blur the frontier and snuff out a conflict that killed 3,200 in 28 years.

Britain and Ireland said that Sinn Fein could join the talks when they resume in September providing the IRA end its guerrilla war and the so-called punishment beatings that have been its means of policing Catholic communities for decades.

"Obviously we will want to assess the ceasefire with great care. What we and others want to see is an end to violence for good and an irrevocable commitment to peaceful means," Blair said hours after the truce was announced.

Unionists, who have long feared that Britain aims eventually to surrender its troublesome and costly province to Ireland, were suspicious and hostile. Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the hardline Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), hinted at a walkout from the talks. "No Unionist of any standing...will be sitting down along with them (Sinn Fein) ," he told the BBC.
The UUP's Ken Maginnis said his party leader wanted reassurance that the IRA would surrender at some stage the arms that have been its chief means of political persuasion.

Maginnis said: "Tony Blair needs to tell us that side by side, at the same time as substantive political negotiations, there will be substantive disarmament, otherwise the whole exercise will be futile and we will have to tell him that."
Mo Mowlam, Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, said she knew that Unionists would be angry at the fact that Sinn Fein can take part in the talks while its IRA backers are armed.

"They (Unionists) are in a difficult position on decommissioning. I think it is important for us to acknowledge that, and then we will do what we can to try to reassure them, to show what the talks process can hold for them," she said.

Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern said he understood the Unionists' feelings and added: "But isn't the absence of violence far better than listening to news of people being shot in their beds and people being blown up,?"
